title: Draupadi's question
hook: a messenger walks to Draupadi's door and comes back carrying a question: whom did you lose first?
carry: whom did you lose first, yourself or me

segments.voice: Yesterday the last stakes fell: the twins, Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira himself, and then Draupadi. A week that ran from Duryodhana's stumble in Maya's hall to the last stake in the dice hall. Your line was name it plainly, the way he did.

The game is over, and Duryodhana wants Draupadi brought into the hall. First he tells Vidura to fetch her. Vidura refuses flatly. In the telling, he says she can't have become anyone's slave, because Yudhishthira staked her after he'd already lost himself. Hold on to that; it's the thread of everything that follows. So Duryodhana turns to an usher, a servant whose job is carrying messages, and sends him to the women's rooms.
screen: `VIDURA REFUSES TO FETCH HER.` → `HE LOST HIMSELF FIRST.` → `A MESSENGER AT HER DOOR.`

segments.voice: The usher tells Draupadi what has happened: Yudhishthira, carried away by the game, has lost her to Duryodhana, and she must come. Draupadi doesn't come. She sends him back to put one thing to the gambler in the hall: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? It's a precise question. If he lost himself first, he was no longer free when he staked her, and perhaps had nothing left to stake. If he staked her first, the answer is different. She isn't pleading. She's asking for the facts the whole claim rests on. The usher asks it in the hall. And Yudhishthira says nothing. The telling says he sits as if he's lost his senses, and answers not a word, good or bad. Duryodhana tells the usher: let her come here and ask it herself. The usher goes back, uneasy, and Draupadi sends him again, this time with a question for everyone: ask the assembly what is right for me to do, and I'll do it. First it was for one man. Now it's for a whole hall of kings and elders. The usher, caught between a furious prince and a woman who won't be moved, hesitates to go a third time. So Duryodhana sends his brother Duhshasana instead. The question, still unanswered, is about to walk into the hall in person.
screen: `THE USHER: YOU'VE BEEN LOST.` · `WHOM DID YOU LOSE FIRST?` · `YUDHISHTHIRA SAYS NOTHING.` · `ASK THE WHOLE ASSEMBLY.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION GROWS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a question you've wanted to ask but haven't, about a decision made for you, or something that didn't add up. Don't answer it; just let it take shape as plainly as Draupadi's did, who decided, on what grounds, and breathe with it. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer; if not, let it sit with you in the quiet.
Draupadi's question. Sent back with a messenger: whom did you lose first, yourself or me? Then sent to the whole hall.
Your line: whom did you lose first, yourself or me. One plain question, and a whole hall has to face it. That's the week.

howItsDone: Draupadi's question is retold in homes, dance and theater, and it's discussed by readers and commentators as a question about dharma and law that the epic leaves open.

original.note: Sanskrit praśna: a question; also the name of the Prashna Upanishad, built on questions.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman refusing to come.
what it means: a woman asking for the facts the whole claim rests on: whom did you lose first?
what a scholar hears: the question turns on whether a man who has lost himself still owns anything to stake, a point of law the hall will argue over.

chat.says: What was Draupadi actually asking when she sent the messenger back?
options: Whom did you lose first, yourself or me? If he'd lost himself, could he still stake her?
She asked the hall to let her husbands play one more game to win her back.
She asked Duryodhana to forgive the debt for the sake of the family.
chat.meaning: Draupadi asked whom Yudhishthira lost first. If he lost himself first, he may have had nothing left to stake.

Draupadi.meaning: the princess married to the five Pandava brothers

Vidura.meaning: the blind king's half-brother and wise counselor

Duryodhana.meaning: eldest of the Kaurava cousins, rival of the Pandavas
